title_content.content: Topic of the Month: 2026 DM Quant Equity Mid-Year Outlook: Factors for an AI and Energy-Led Cycle

paragraph_content.content: This month, we present our mid-year outlook for quant equities in the US, Europe and Japan. We recap the views of our economists (here) and strategists (here) as a starting point to highlight the equity factors that are likely to stand out in this environment.

The first half of 2026 has reinforced a familiar but more complex market message: macro and micro fundamentals remain supportive for risk assets, but return dispersion is likely to stay elevated. Strong earnings reports, resilient US labor markets and a powerful AI-driven capex cycle continue to support developed market equities. At the same time, energy-led volatility, driven by the Middle East conflict and uncertainty around the duration of the supply shock, has widened the range of potential macro outcomes. In this environment, the core message from our global strategists is constructive, not complacent.

DM equities remain the asset class preferred by our cross-asset strategists (here), with expected returns in the low-teens across major developed regions. While upside appears broadly similar across the US, Europe and Japan, our strategists prefer the US given its favorable bull-bear skew, stronger earnings profile and support from positive operating leverage. Europe and Japan also offer upside, but with more region-specific constraints: Europe is more exposed to energy-price volatility, faster pass-through into inflation and a different ECB reaction function, while Japan's outlook hinges on energy costs, wage growth, governance reform and sector leadership tied to AI, materials and defense.

The most important macro uncertainty is the oil-price path. Our economists note that the level and duration of the Middle East-related supply shock will dictate economic outcomes, with growth and inflation elasticities becoming increasingly non-linear as oil prices rise and remain elevated. The base case assumes de-escalation, but the range of outcomes is wider than usual. In the US, higher energy prices act as a tax on consumption, partially offsetting fiscal support, but AI capex and resilient labor markets keep the economy on a constructive path. In Europe, energy-price pass-through is faster and more direct, leaving the ECB with a different reaction function from the Fed. In Japan, higher energy prices create pressure on margins, but the broader equity story remains supported by domestic reflation, structural capex demand and improving corporate governance.

Across regions, one common thread remains central: the AI capex cycle. Hyperscaler capex expectations have been revised sharply higher, and the investment impulse from AI infrastructure is now relevant not only for technology and communication services, but also for semiconductors, industrials, utilities, power equipment, robotics, data centers and parts of credit and securitized markets. For quant investors, this reinforces the importance of factors that combine earnings delivery, quality, valuation discipline, cash-flow resilience and positive revisions.

Against this backdrop, our regional factor recommendations are as follows. In the US, we continue to emphasize Internal Growth, Low PEG, and Up vs. Down EPS Revisions, reflecting a preference for quality growth, valuation-aware earnings growth and positive earnings momentum. In Europe, we recommend Operating Cash Flow Yield, Low YoY Asset Growth, and 3-Month Up vs. Down EPS Revisions Breadth, reflecting the need for cash-flow resilience, capital discipline and earnings selectivity in an energy-sensitive market. In Japan, we recommend Forward Earnings Yield, Low PEG, and Up vs. Down EPS Revisions, combining value exposure, valuation-aware earnings growth and bottom-up earnings momentum in a rising but more dispersed equity market.

title_content.content: US quant factors – Quality Growth as AI Productivity Cycle Offsets Energy Headwinds

paragraph_content.content: In Exhibit 1, we show the key US forecasts from our economists and strategists for 2026 and 2027. Our economists expect US growth to soften modestly through mid-2026 as higher energy prices weigh on consumption, though AI-driven capex, fiscal support and resilient labor markets should continue to support underlying momentum. On an annual basis, real GDP growth is expected to be 2.2% in 2026 and 2.5% in 2027 as energy pressures fade and the economy avoids recession. Inflation remains above target in the near term, but both headline and core inflation are expected to decelerate over the forecast horizon, allowing the Fed to remain on hold through 2026 before delivering two cuts in 1H27.

Our US equity strategists continue to expect the rolling recovery to progress. The constructive equity view is primarily an earnings story rather than a multiple-expansion story. Positive operating leverage, AI adoption, “run it lean” efficiency gains, improving pricing power and continued momentum in the AI capex cycle are expected to support earnings growth. Sector preferences remain tilted toward Financials, Industrials, Consumer Discretionary Goods and hyperscalers.

paragraph_content.content: Reflecting this combination of resilient earnings, AI-led productivity gains and persistent but moderating inflation pressure, we maintain our preference for Growth with a quality bias. We recommend positioning via three equity factors: Internal Growth, Low PEG, and Up vs. Down EPS Revisions. Together, these factors capture companies with the ability to fund growth internally, combine sustainable growth with valuation discipline, and benefit from positive analyst revisions as productivity gains and pricing power are incorporated into earnings forecasts.

We evaluate this factor mix through three lenses. First, in Exhibit 2, we present the backtested performance of our recommended US factors across rising and flat inflation regimes. Internal Growth and Up vs. Down EPS Revisions remain resilient across both regimes, while Low PEG performs particularly well in flatter inflation environments. This is consistent with the current macro setup: inflation remains a risk, but the direction of travel should become more benign as energy and tariff effects fade, allowing investors to re-focus on earnings quality and growth durability.

Second, in Exhibit 3, we evaluate the performance of our recommended US factors across normal and high Brent oil-volatility regimes. Internal Growth and Low PEG delivered positive returns in both regimes, with stronger performance during high oil volatility, highlighting the resilience of quality-growth and valuation-disciplined growth when energy uncertainty is elevated. Up vs. Down EPS Revisions performed positively in normal oil-volatility regimes but was weaker during high-volatility episodes, potentially because analyst estimates would lag the initial shock as earnings, margin and demand assumptions are recalibrated. This supports a balanced US factor basket: Internal Growth and Low PEG provide resilience during the energy-shock phase, while Up vs. Down EPS Revisions becomes more relevant as oil volatility stabilizes and earnings visibility improves.

Third, in Exhibit 4, we assess the thematic alignment of our recommended factors with the AI & Tech Diffusion main theme and AI Infrastructure sub-theme, measured as the mean exposure of top-quintile stocks minus bottom-quintile stocks. The exhibit shows positive exposure to the AI themes, reinforcing the alignment of our factor recommendations with our US equity strategists' emphasis on AI as a key driver of the earnings cycle. The exposure to AI Infrastructure is particularly relevant as AI-related capex remains an important global theme, with hyperscaler capex expectations revised sharply higher for 2026 and 2027.

paragraph_content.content: Having evaluated the recommended factors across the broader macro and thematic lenses, we now take a more granular view of the supportive characteristics behind each signal. We continue to favor a quality-oriented approach to growth investing, positioning Internal Growth as our preferred factor within the US equity landscape. Internal Growth is explicitly defined as:

Among the growth factors we analyze, Internal Growth distinctly exhibits the strongest positive exposure to quality characteristics, measured as the difference between median Composite Quality scores of top quintile (Q1) and bottom quintile (Q5) portfolios (see Exhibit 5). This notable quality tilt underscores the factor's strategic appeal, identifying companies capable of sustainably funding growth internally through disciplined profitability and effective reinvestment.
To further illustrate the fundamental strengths underlying Internal Growth, we employ the DuPont decomposition framework to expand ROE into its component drivers:

title_content.content: ROE = Profit Margin × Asset Turnover × Financial Leverage

paragraph_content.content: In Exhibit 6, we apply this decomposition by comparing median fundamental exposures of top quintile (Q1) versus bottom quintile (Q5) firms. The top-quintile companies consistently demonstrate superior fundamentals across all key drivers – including notably stronger profit margins and greater asset efficiency, partly offset by lower financial leverage – highlighting their ability to sustain internally funded growth. This aligns with our US equity strategists' view that the rolling recovery is being driven by earnings durability, positive operating leverage and AI-enabled efficiency gains. Internal Growth is well suited to that backdrop because it captures companies with the profitability and retained earnings capacity to fund expansion internally.

paragraph_content.content: As a complement to Internal Growth, Low PEG adds valuation discipline to the quality-growth framework. The Low PEG factor identifies companies with attractive valuations relative to their earnings growth trajectories.

Exhibit 7 shows the rolling 252-day correlation of Low PEG with Composite Value and Composite Growth. Low PEG has recently shown a higher correlation with Composite Growth than Composite Value, which is particularly relevant in the current US backdrop. Our strategists expect modest multiple compression, with the S&P 500 forward P/E declining to 20.5x from 21.2x, making their bullish index view an earnings story rather than multiple-expansion (see report). In this environment, a stronger relationship with Growth is preferable to a Value tilt, because returns are expected to come more from earnings delivery than from a broad re-rating of cheap stocks.

The factor is currently screening at an attractive valuation (Exhibit 8), trading at the 12th percentile of its historical range. In our view, the combination of growth sensitivity, valuation discipline and supportive starting valuations makes Low PEG well suited for an earnings-led market environment.

paragraph_content.content: Finally, Up vs. Down EPS Revisions adds a forward-looking earnings momentum signal to our US factor recommendation. The factor measures analyst upgrades relative to downgrades, normalized by the total number of analyst estimates, and captures the bottom-up channel through which improving earnings expectations are reflected in stock selection. This factor remains highly relevant as consensus incorporates three competing forces into forecasts: AI-driven productivity gains, improving pricing power, and inflation shocks from energy. In our view, revisions should remain one of the most direct channels through which the earnings-led recovery is reflected in quant performance.

In Exhibit 9, we track the proportion of US stocks experiencing upward revisions in NTM earnings relative to downgrades on a monthly basis. 56% of stocks now have net positive earnings revisions, compared with 37% facing net downgrades, signaling broadening optimism in analyst sentiment and earnings expectations.

Exhibit 10 provides additional support for this fundamental outlook, illustrating median factor scores for key attributes by comparing top-quintile stocks (Q1) versus bottom-quintile stocks (Q5). Stocks in the top quintile demonstrate notably higher operating leverage, stronger net margin trends, and greater investment intensity in R&D. Specifically, elevated operating leverage – defined as the 12-month change in EBIT divided by the 12-month change in sales – and superior net margin momentum – defined precisely as (Current Net Margin – 5-year average Net Margin) divided by the 5-year standard deviation of Net Margin – reinforce these companies' capacity to benefit directly from recovering pricing power and operational efficiencies. Additionally, higher R&D investment (relative to sales) among top-quintile firms aligns directly with our strategists' emphasis on innovation and AI-driven productivity enhancements, further underpinning their competitive advantage and sustainable earnings growth potential.

Internal Growth provides the high-quality expression of AI-enabled productivity; Low PEG balances growth with valuation discipline; and Up vs. Down EPS Revisions captures the broadening of earnings strength as the recovery continues.

title_content.content: Europe quant factors – Positioning for Energy-Driven Inflation With Cash-Flow Resilience, Capital Discipline and Earnings Revisions

paragraph_content.content: In Exhibit 11, we show the key forecasts from our economists and strategists in Europe for 2026 and 2027. Our economists expect a temporary euro area growth slowdown driven by higher energy prices, with Europe more exposed than the US given the region's faster pass-through of energy costs into inflation and activity. However, they do not expect a prolonged downturn in the baseline scenario, assuming energy volatility gradually subsides and growth stabilizes into 2027. Europe's quick pass-through of energy costs to core inflation and growth means it may see the largest near-term sensitivity to the energy shock. Persistent dual exposure to oil and LNG is likely to keep core inflation stubbornly elevated, broadly unchanged at
in both 2026 and 2027. The ECB is expected to deliver two additional 25bp rate hikes in 2026 before policy gradually converges back toward neutral in 2027.

Against this macro backdrop, our European equity strategists continue to see upside for MSCI Europe through mid-2027, with a target of 2,700. However, European equities are expected to remain choppy in the near term, particularly as sentiment remains tied to developments around the Strait of Hormuz and energy markets. While earnings have so far proven resilient, upside is more back-end loaded and more dependent on Energy, sector selection and stock-specific momentum than in the US. At the same time, our strategists continue to see underappreciated AI productivity opportunities in Europe, particularly through Semis and select AI-related pockets of Capital Goods and Materials & Mining. Our strategists note that Germany's fiscal spend is tracking below annual targets in both Defence and Infrastructure, while a potential restart of more tangible Russia/Ukraine negotiations remains worth monitoring as an upside risk into year-end. From a sector perspective, our strategists prefer European Semis, Utilities, Tobacco, Energy, Banks and Telecoms.

These factors reflect a more defensive and selective approach than in the US, consistent with an environment shaped by energy-driven inflation, slower near-term growth and more hawkish ECB policy. The focus is on companies with resilient cash generation, disciplined capital allocation and positive earnings momentum in a market where energy inflation and central bank policy can quickly pressure margins.

We evaluate the recommended factors through three lenses: inflation, oil volatility and energy-theme exposure. First, in Exhibit 12, we show performance across rising and flat inflation regimes. All three factors deliver positive returns in both regimes, supporting a balanced factor positioning for an environment where inflation and policy uncertainty remain tied to energy prices.

Second, Exhibit 13 evaluates performance across normal and high Brent oil-volatility regimes. This is directly relevant to the Europe outlook, where our strategists note that earnings have so far proven resilient, but that a persistent Strait of Hormuz disruption could broaden downside risks. Operating Cash Flow Yield performs positively in both regimes and is strongest when oil volatility is high, reinforcing its role as a cash-flow resilience factor when energy costs can pressure margins and activity. Low YoY Asset Growth also performs positively across both regimes, consistent with the value of capital discipline in an energy-uncertain backdrop. 3M Up vs. Down EPS Revisions is weaker in high oil volatility but performs strongly in normal regimes, suggesting that revisions become more useful as volatility stabilizes and analysts have better visibility on margins, demand and earnings momentum.

Finally, Exhibit 14 shows net thematic exposure to the Future of Energy main theme and Energy Security sub-theme, calculated as top-quintile mean exposure minus bottom-quintile mean exposure. This is particularly relevant for Europe, where energy sensitivity and supply disruption risk remain central to our strategists' outlook. Positive exposure across the recommended factors supports their relevance in an energy-sensitive market, while adding alignment with longer-term themes around energy resilience and security of supply.

The Operating Cash Flow Yield factor targets companies with superior cash-generation capabilities, stable margins and resilient operating profiles. In Europe, where energy-price volatility can affect both demand and input costs, cash-flow durability is especially valuable. The factor is well suited to an environment in which broad-based earnings upside may be constrained, but companies with strong internal cash generation can continue to defend margins, fund operations and maintain shareholder returns.

In Exhibit 15, we show the factor's cumulative performance and 126-day rolling Sharpe ratio. Operating Cash Flow Yield delivered strong cumulative returns through 2025 and early 2026, followed by a modest dip around March, before beginning to recover into April. The rolling Sharpe ratio remains elevated, reinforcing the factor's defensive quality in a market where energy costs and macro uncertainty can pressure margins and activity. In Exhibit 16, we show the factor's current valuation relative to history. Operating Cash Flow Yield is trading at the 23rd percentile relative to its history since 1990, suggesting that valuation support remains reasonable despite recent performance strength.

In Exhibit 17 we show the factor's sector composition by comparing the number of top-quintile and bottom-quintile stocks across sectors. The factor shows positive net exposure to Communication Services, Energy, Consumer Discretionary, Consumer Staples, Utilities and Materials, and negative net exposure to Industrials, Information Technology and Health Care. Positive exposure to Utilities and Consumer Staples highlights the factor's defensive, cash-resilient profile, while positive exposure to Energy reinforces its relevance in a market shaped by energy sensitivity and oil-volatility risk.

paragraph_content.content: We also favor Low YoY Asset Growth as a capital-discipline factor within our Europe recommendations. The factor is defined as the annual percentage change in total assets, with a preference for lower values. From a fundamental perspective, it captures companies that avoid aggressive balance-sheet expansion and invest more selectively. In an environment where energy volatility can pressure margins, demand and funding conditions, markets are likely to place greater value on disciplined capital allocation and a more cautious approach to growth.

In Exhibit 18, we evaluate Low YoY Asset Growth across 2-year yield regimes. The factor performs best when 2-year yields are rising, consistent with the idea that capital discipline becomes more valuable as front-end rates move higher and the cost of capital increases. This is particularly relevant in Europe, where our economists expect the ECB to deliver two additional 25bp rate hikes in 2026 before policy gradually converges back toward neutral in 2027.

In Exhibit 19, we show the current average cost of equity across quintiles of the Asset Growth factor. While the relationship is not perfectly monotonic, the broader pattern is clear: currently firms in higher asset-growth buckets tend to face a higher cost of equity than low asset-growth firms. This supports the case for disciplined asset growth in a higher-rate environment, where aggressive balance-sheet expansion is more likely to be penalized.

Finally, the factor's supportive tilts toward Energy and Materials (see Exhibit 20) are also notable in the current European context, where energy-related earnings and cash flows are more relevant to regional index-level earnings growth than in the US.

title_content.content: Japan quant factors – A Dual Approach Integrating Macroeconomic and Micro-Level Insight

paragraph_content.content: In Exhibit 24, we show the key forecasts from our economists and strategists in Japan for 2026 and 2027. Our equity strategists expect the rally in Japanese equities to continue, with TOPIX projected to reach 4,300 by June 2027. The market remains supported by Japan's ongoing transition toward a more reflationary environment, structural labor shortages, wage growth, productivity-enhancing capex, corporate governance reform and strategic investments tied to AI, semiconductors, power infrastructure, defense, robotics and telecoms.

Meanwhile, our macro strategists expect long-term interest rates, which have been trending higher on the back of Bank of Japan rate hikes, to see a modest short-term decline but remain broadly range-bound over the medium term. This creates a supportive backdrop for value factors, particularly if rates do not decline materially. At the same time, higher oil prices can pressure corporate profitability, increasing the importance of valuation metrics tied directly to earnings and of bottom-up revisions as a stock-selection signal.

paragraph_content.content: In this environment, we recommend the following three factors for Japanese equities: Up vs. Down EPS Revisions, Forward Earnings Yield, and Low PEG. The first is primarily driven by company-level micro factors, while the latter two are strategies focused mainly on macro considerations.
The Up vs. Down EPS Revisions factor involves taking long positions in stocks that analysts have upgraded and short positions in those that have been downgraded in terms of earnings forecasts.
Japan's earnings revision breadth turned downward following the U.S.-Iran conflict in

March 2026 and has recently been hovering around zero (Exhibit 25). Guidance for the new fiscal year also shows increasing divergence, with a clear split between companies that are effectively managing rising oil prices and those that are not (Japan Is Back, Still Climbing: The Summit Lies Ahead (12 May, 2026)). In other words, the gap between these groups of companies at the earnings level has become more pronounced, suggesting that earnings-driven stock selection is becoming increasingly important. Note that the earnings revision breadth refers to FY1 here, as the most recent guidance from companies with March fiscal year-ends is reflected in FY1 estimates.

Meanwhile, foreign investor flows into Japanese equities remain robust (Exhibit 26). Based on our analysis, there is a positive correlation between foreign investor flows into cash equity and the momentum factor (Quant Matters Japan (Jun 2025) (18 Jun, 2025)). The revision factor, which broadly falls within the momentum category, is no exception. Against the backdrop of Japan's ongoing normalization, we expect continued strong foreign inflows into Japanese equities, and therefore believe the revision factor is likely to deliver solid performance over the medium term.

European equities rebounded in April, with the Euro Stoxx rising 5.5%, supported by relief following the US-Iran ceasefire and a broader global risk-on backdrop. However, concerns around growth and inflation remained elevated amid higher energy prices. Euro Area activity data weakened sharply, with the composite PMI falling to 48.6 in April from 50.7 in March, reflecting broad-based softness across countries (see report). According to our economists, services activity is beginning to feel the impact of the energy shock, although manufacturing remained relatively resilient, with the manufacturing PMI rising to 52.2. Inflation remained mixed, with headline HICP rising to 3.0% YoY while core eased to 2.2% YoY (see report). According to our economists, further upside from energy prices remains likely. The ECB kept rates unchanged in April, while highlighting rising upside risks to inflation and downside risks to growth (see report). In the UK, activity data proved more resilient, with the composite PMI rising to 52.0 and monthly GDP increasing 0.5% m/m in February (see reports here and here).

April saw European factor performance supported by a broader global risk-on environment, despite ongoing concerns around growth and inflation. Sentiment improved early in the month following optimism around a potential Middle East ceasefire, supporting a rebound in European equities, while oil prices fell sharply before rebounding later as negotiations stalled. The recovery in markets came despite a weaker macro backdrop, with Euro Area PMIs deteriorating sharply and the ECB emphasizing rising downside risks to growth alongside persistent inflation concerns. Sector performance was broadly positive, with 9 out of 11 sectors delivering gains. Information Technology led the region with a strong +16.6% return, followed by Industrials (+11.0%) and Financials (+10.8%), while Energy (-2.1%) and Communication Services (-0.8%) lagged. Factor leadership also shifted meaningfully from March, with Momentum extending its rebound as risk appetite improved. Against this backdrop, Composite Value posted modest gains (+0.1%), as weakness in Energy and easing oil prices early in the month offset support from improving cyclical sentiment and rising risk appetite. Its net negative exposure to Industrials—one of the strongest-performing sectors during the month—acted as a relative headwind. In contrast, Composite Growth rose modestly (+0.3%), benefiting from the strong rebound in Information Technology and renewed optimism around AI and global equities, although gains remained muted relative to the US given the weaker Euro Area macro backdrop. The gap between Value and Growth narrowed significantly relative to March, when Composite Value had risen 4.4% while Composite Growth had declined 4.0% amid the energy shock and rising rates environment. Composite Quality declined 0.5%, as the rebound in higher-beta cyclical and technology sectors reduced investor preference for defensive and stable earnings exposures. Composite Momentum outperformed strongly (+5.4%), extending the positive momentum seen in March, as continued strength in technology and cyclical sectors reinforced prevailing return trends and supported trend-following exposures. Size (Small) fell 0.7%, with smaller caps continuing to lag as tighter financial conditions, weaker PMIs, and softer growth expectations weighed on more domestically exposed companies. Low Volatility fell 3.7%, as investors rotated away from defensive positioning back toward higher-beta exposures.

paragraph_content.content: US equities rebounded strongly in April, with the S&P 500 rising 10.5% following the sharp March selloff. US data were generally firm. Payrolls rose 178k in March and the unemployment rate declined to 4.26% (see report), easing immediate Fed concerns around labor market weakness. ISM Manufacturing remained in expansionary territory at 52.7, while ISM Services moderated to 54.0 (see reports here and here). Core PCE inflation rose 0.37% m/m in February, marking a third consecutive month above 0.3% m/m, although our economists expect deceleration ahead (see report). Consumer sentiment weakened sharply, with preliminary University of Michigan sentiment falling to 47.6 (see report), while March retail sales remained strong, with headline sales rising 1.7% m/m and control group sales up 0.7% (see report). The Fed left rates unchanged, though the statement reflected a more hawkish tone and reduced easing bias (see report). Meanwhile, 1Q GDP rose 2.0%, with underlying domestic demand stronger than expected (see report).

April saw a sharp reversal in US factor leadership as improving sentiment around corporate earnings, artificial intelligence (AI), and semiconductors drove a strong rebound in risk appetite following the March selloff. Sentiment improved as macro data remained resilient and oil prices stabilized somewhat despite ongoing Middle East tensions, while a supportive earnings season further reinforced the recovery in risk appetite. Sector performance was broadly positive, with 9 out of 11 sectors delivering positive returns. Communication Services (+18.4%) led gains, followed by Information Technology (+17.4%) and Consumer Discretionary (+11.5%), while Energy (-3.5%) and Healthcare (-0.5%) lagged. Meanwhile, the 10-year US Treasury yield ended slightly higher at 4.39% versus 4.32% the previous month. Against this backdrop, Composite Value declined sharply (-10.0%), reversing part of its strong March outperformance as leadership rotated away from energy and defensive cyclicals toward growth-oriented sectors. Weakness in Energy, alongside Value's lower exposure to technology and AI-linked names, weighed materially on performance. In contrast, Composite Growth rebounded strongly (+7.0%), benefiting from renewed strength in large-cap technology, semiconductors, and AI-related equities as investors rotated back toward longer-duration exposures. Composite Quality gained 1.5%, supported primarily by its strong long exposure to Information Technology, which was among the best-performing sectors during the month. Its underweight exposure to Communication Services partially offset gains, given the sector's strong performance.

Composite Momentum was the strongest performer, rising 14.4%, as the sharp rebound in technology and communication services reinforced prevailing return trends and supported trend-following exposures. Small Size declined 0.6%, with smaller caps continuing to lag despite the broader equity recovery, as investors remained focused on larger, more liquid growth names. Low Volatility fell sharply (−12.8%), as investors rotated aggressively away from defensive positioning and back into higher-beta risk exposures.

title_content.content: Factor Contribution to Market Performance – April 2026

paragraph_content.content: In this section, we analyse the contribution of key equity factors to market performance using both factor sensitivities (betas) and a realised return decomposition framework. We estimate factor exposures by regressing monthly total returns (in USD) of the MSCI US, MSCI Europe and MSCI Japan indices against six key factor return series over a rolling 36-month window, providing a more robust view of each market's structural factor tilts (Exhibit 51).

We then translate these exposures into realised contributions by combining factor betas with the latest month's factor returns, allowing us to assess how each style factor influenced overall market performance (see Exhibit 52). The residual non-style effects – defined as the market return minus the sum of the contributions from all six key factors – capture the portion of returns driven by broader market, sectoral and idiosyncratic effects.

In April, global equity markets rebounded strongly following the sharp declines seen in March, supported by easing geopolitical concerns and improving risk sentiment. In USD terms, the MSCI Europe gained 7.3%, the MSCI US rose 10.5%, and the MSCI Japan advanced 9.1%.

In Europe, factor contributions were broadly positive but relatively muted compared to other regions. Momentum was the primary positive driver, suggesting that recent outperformers continued to lead during the recovery. Low Volatility also contributed meaningfully, consistent with continued demand for defensive positioning even as markets rallied. Quality added modestly, while Value and Growth had negligible contributions. Size (Small) was a minor detractor, indicating limited headwinds from smaller-cap exposure. The residual non-style component remained the largest contributor, reflecting the dominance of broader market and idiosyncratic effects.

The US market displayed the strongest factor-driven performance profile. Momentum emerged as the dominant positive contributor, reflecting strong trend persistence and supportive factor returns during the month. Low Volatility also contributed substantially, suggesting that defensive characteristics were well-rewarded despite the risk-on environment. In contrast, Value was the primary detractor, indicating that valuation dynamics weighed on performance, while Quality also dragged modestly. Size (Small) had a limited negative impact, and Growth contributions were negligible. Notably, the residual component was slightly negative, suggesting that systematic factor effects dominated market movements in the US this month.

In Japan, factor contributions were pronounced, with notable divergence between positive and negative drivers. Low Volatility was the strongest positive contributor, reflecting meaningful outperformance of lower-volatility segments. Momentum also added substantially, indicating continued trend-following dynamics. Value contributed positively, suggesting a supportive environment for lower-valuation stocks. Growth was a marginal positive. However, Size (Small) was a significant detractor, indicating that smaller-cap stocks underperformed meaningfully during the period. Quality was also a drag, consistent with challenges for higher-quality segments. The residual component was modestly negative, suggesting that systematic factor exposures largely explained performance.

Overall, while factor exposures highlight persistent structural tilts across regions, the realised contributions emphasise a notable shift from March, with Momentum and Low Volatility emerging as key positive drivers across all three markets. Regional divergence remains evident: Europe saw more balanced contributions with a significant residual component; the US benefited from exceptionally strong Momentum effects offset by Value weakness; and Japan experienced pronounced factor contributions in both directions – with Low Volatility, Momentum and Value providing support, while Size and Quality posed meaningful headwinds.

paragraph_content.content: We calculate the Sharpe ratios of a long-short quintile portfolio over four horizons, namely long-term (i.e. since 1990) (LT), past 10 years (10Y), past 1 year (1Y), and past 1 month (1M). We prefer factors with higher Sharpe ratios.

We take the median of the price-to-book ratio of all equities in the factor long holdings divided by the median price-to-book ratio of the equities in the factor short holdings, and we calculate the same ratio based on forward P/E. The ratios of the book-to-price (BP) ratio and the forward earnings yield (EPF) are then averaged. We determine the valuation level for each factor based on its time series percentiles since 1990. We prefer factors with cheap valuation percentile.

Earnings Revision Ratio (ERR): The signal is defined as the 3-month average of the number of upward EPS revisions minus the number of downward EPS revisions, divided by the total number of analyst estimates for the upcoming fiscal year. The ratio is averaged for the last three months. Then we take the spread of the median ERR of the factor top quintile minus the factor bottom quintile. We determine a net ERR of a factor in terms of percentiles over the factor's own history since 1990.

Price Z-Score (PRICE): The signal is defined as the one-year rolling z-score of the daily factor performance. The z-score is a contrarian signal at its extremes, it detects when a factor is overbought or oversold relative to history.

Exposure: We would prefer factors with lower sensitivity to country, industry and market beta. We quantify the country (CTRY) and industry (INDU) exposures by the sum of the top four net overweight or underweight countries and industries in absolute value. We calculate the net beta (BETA) as the absolute spread between the top and bottom factor quintile beta.

Macro: We focus on four macro indicators, namely economic cycles (ECO), equity risk premium (ERP), inflation (INF), and long-term interest rate (YIELD). For each macro indicator, we calculate the average factor return in a certain regime against the average return over the entire history. Then we perform a Welch's T-test and calculate the t-statistics to evaluate the significance of the relative performance.

Within Efficacy, Valuation, Sentiment and Exposure, each component inside carries equal weight. Within the dimension of Macro, economic cycles carry the same weight as the combination of equity risk premium, inflation and long-term interest rate. To consolidate, we determine the combined ranking by assigning 20% to each of the Efficacy, Valuation, Sentiment, Macro, and Exposures dimensions.
